newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries end mostly flat after late buying.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries end mostly flat after late buying.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries ended little changed on Thursday, as a late bout of short-covering brought the market off lows that prevailed for most of the session.

The 30-year bond closed at 99-10/32, up 4/32 from Wednesday. Its yield edged down to 6.68 percent, its lowest level since the 6.66 percent seen on February 25 close. On Wednesday, the 30-year yield ended at 6.69 percent.
"I don't know what is going to cause the market to go down between now and the quarter end" on June 30, said Richard Schwarz, a senior trader at Zions First National Bank.
Schwarz said he expects the market to remain at the lofty levels that have been seen for more than a week. But he and other traders said they do not expect Treasuries to rally much further.
"I think the market has gone as far as it can go," said a trader at a U.S. primary dealer.

He noted the short-end of the yield curve in particular has been capped, with the two-year note's yield hovering around 6.0 percent with it unlikely to break below that level unless economic data turn very weak.
Treasuries, though, moved higher early on Thursday, gaining more than a 1/4-point after the Labor Department reported jobless claims rose 8,000 to 347,000 in the week ended June 14.

But those gains were short-lived because the Federal Reserve of Philadelphia said that its business activity index soared to 25.2 in June from 1.6 in May. Indices for new and unfilled orders, delivery time inventories and employment also rose sharply.
The prices paid index fell to 15.0 in June from 16.2 in May, but prices received rose to 3.1 from -0.7.

Treasury prices quickly fell on the strong data, but traders said it was mostly day-traders setting up short positions in the anticipation Treasuries would fall even more during the session. That didn't happen and Treasuries stuck to very tight ranges until late in the session.

"They were getting no satisfaction so they covered their shorts," Schwarz said, noting the day-traders likely did not want to carry those positions overnight. "They were hoping for follow-through on the downside but they didn't get it."
Rather, traders said, retail buying kept the market from dropping further.
With the exception of the buying after the claims numbers and selling after the Philadelphia Fed survey, activity was very light.

"The market is tired; it is running out of room on the upside," said Richard Gilhooly, Treasury market strategist at Paribas Corp. "The market is putting in a top and we expect it to go down next week."
Gilhooly deemed the market "overbought," as the market becomes more bullish.
He explained that much of the buying was not from new cash, but rather from people extending out the curve.

Helping the market late in the day was a successful $13.0 billion 52-week bill auction, sold an average discount rate of 5.35 percent. Non-competitve bids were a robust $977 million and the bid-to-cover ratio was high at 4.71.
Players said they anticipate a quiet day on Friday, with no key economic data scheduled. The lone piece of news is the May federal budget statement, due at 1400 EDT/1800 GMT.

As of 1500 EDT Thursday, trading volume was $75 billion, seven percent below an average Thursday in the second quarter, according to GovPX. Bill volume was 30 percent below average, while coupon volume was seven percent above average.

Late on Thursday, two-year notes were unchanged at 100-14/32 to yield 6.01 percent. Five-year notes were unchanged at 100-29/32 to yield 6.28 percent and the 10-year note was up 1/32 to 101-22/32 to yield 6.39 percent.
Three-month bill rates were steady at 4.94 percent, six-month rates were up one basis point at 5.08 percent and year bill rates were up one basis point at 5.34 percent.
Early in the session, the market shrugged off a 7.8 percent widening of the U.S. trade deficit in April to $8.36 billion, from a revised $7.76 billion gap in March.
